title: Rare Events Govern Defect Formation Under Weak Symmetry Breaking
authors: Jiang Liu, Peng Yang, Matteo Baggioli
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Crossing a continuous phase transition out of equilibrium typically generates topological defects whose density obeys a universal power-law scaling predicted by the Kibble-Zurek mechanism. Recent numerical studies have revealed systematic deviations from this scaling in the presence of weak explicit symmetry breaking, manifested as an additional exponential suppression of defect formation. However, the origin of this correction and a general theoretical framework to describe it have remained elusive. Here, using large-deviation theory, we show that defect formation under weak symmetry breaking is controlled by rare fluctuations that drive local regions into the disfavored symmetry-broken state. This mechanism yields a closed-form expression for the defect density in arbitrary dimensions, valid in the weak-field and weak-noise limits. These theoretical predictions are verified through direct simulations of stochastic Ginzburg-Landau models in one and two spatial dimensions.
tldr: Defect formation under weak symmetry breaking is governed by rare fluctuations, leading to an exponential correction to the Kibble-Zurek scaling.
motivation: Systematic deviations from the Kibble-Zurek mechanism have been observed in numerical studies of phase transitions with weak explicit symmetry breaking, but a theoretical explanation was missing.
method: The authors apply large-deviation theory to derive a closed-form expression for defect density in arbitrary dimensions, valid in weak-field and weak-noise limits, and verify it with stochastic Ginzburg-Landau simulations.
result: The defect density exhibits an exponential suppression factor beyond the Kibble-Zurek power law, controlled by rare fluctuations that locally drive the system into the disfavored symmetry-broken state.
conclusion: Rare events are the key mechanism behind defect formation under weak symmetry breaking, providing a general theoretical framework that matches simulations.

title: End-to-End Learning Of Quantum Control On Latent Dynamical Manifold
authors: Jun-Dong Zhong, Zong-Yuan Ge, Feng-Hua Ren, Zhao-Ming Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional quantum control relies on an iterative "simulate-then-optimize" paradigm, where dynamics simulation and control design are decoupled, leading to substantial computational overhead and limited scalability, particularly in noisy environments. Here, we propose an end-to-end quantum control framework based on long short-term memory, in which system dynamics and control strategies are learned jointly in a low dimensional latent manifold. The model directly maps initial states and environmental parameters to both dynamical trajectories and optimized control pulse in a single forward pass. The framework is validated on adiabatic speedup in a two-level system and state transfer in a one-dimensional spin chain under noise, achieving accurate dynamical prediction and control optimization. It improves the fidelity for both tasks and significantly reduces the optimization cost by three orders of magnitude compared with conventional iterative methods, while exhibiting strong generalization to multi-parameter, time-varying noise, as well as to different initial states and driving fields. Our work introduces a data-driven control paradigm based on latent manifold learning, reducing the computational bottleneck of iterative optimization and enabling real-time adaptive control of complex open quantum systems.
tldr: An end-to-end LSTM-based framework jointly learns quantum dynamics and control in a latent manifold, achieving fast and robust control for open quantum systems.
motivation: Traditional quantum control methods are computationally expensive and scale poorly, especially in noisy environments. The authors aim to reduce the computational bottleneck by learning dynamics and control jointly.
method: They use a long short-term memory (LSTM) network to map initial states and environmental parameters directly to dynamical trajectories and optimized control pulses in a single forward pass, operating in a low-dimensional latent manifold.
result: The framework improves fidelity for adiabatic speedup and state transfer tasks, reduces optimization cost by three orders of magnitude, and generalizes well to multi-parameter time-varying noise and different initial conditions.
conclusion: This data-driven approach enables real-time adaptive control of complex open quantum systems, significantly reducing computational overhead and enhancing scalability.

title: Hard-core Bosons In Action: Applications To Quantum Circuits
authors: Michael Epping David Emmanuel-Costa
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The use of algebraic frameworks based on complex Clifford algebras for the representation and simulation of quantum circuits has been discussed in the literature. Recently, an alternative algebraic approach employing hard-core bosons has been proposed. Hard-core bosons provide a natural representation of multi-qubit systems, in which the tensor-product structure is realized directly and no sign corrections are required, in contrast to realizations based on complex Clifford algebras. Although both approaches are formally equivalent, the hard-core boson formulation exhibits computational advantages. This work reviews and extends the hard-core boson algebra for circuit simulation and presents an efficient implementation. A performance comparison with IBM Qiskit shows substantially improved execution times for simulations. Moreover, a new application is introduced in which the hard-core boson formalism is combined with genetic algorithms for quantum circuit synthesis.
tldr: This paper reviews and extends a hard-core boson algebra for quantum circuit simulation, demonstrating improved execution times over IBM Qiskit and introducing a genetic algorithm for circuit synthesis.
motivation: Efficient simulation and synthesis of quantum circuits are important for quantum computing research, and alternative algebraic frameworks may offer computational advantages.
method: The authors review the hard-core boson representation of multi-qubit systems, implement it efficiently, and combine it with genetic algorithms for circuit synthesis.
result: The hard-core boson implementation shows substantially improved execution times compared to IBM Qiskit, and the genetic algorithm approach enables circuit synthesis.
conclusion: The hard-core boson formalism is a promising tool for quantum circuit simulation and synthesis, with practical performance benefits.

title: I-QMapper: Error-Aware Layout Optimization And Device Diagnostics For Nisq Hardware
authors: Kenneth Merz Milana Bazayeva
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Achieving high-fidelity execution on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware requires careful selection of physical qubit layouts, as gate errors, readout errors, and coherence times vary across the device and drift over time. Currently, qubit mapping is performed either through manual inspection of device calibration data or through automated layout pipelines, neither of which provides integrated, interactive layout visualization combined with calibration analytics. In this work, we present the Interactive Quantum Mapper (I-QMapper), a Jupyter-based, open-source tool for noise-aware layout selection, visualization, and analysis on superconducting quantum hardware. I-QMapper offers two operating modes: a general-purpose mode for arbitrary circuits, and a dedicated mode for quantum-chemistry applications, specifically tailored to the Local Unitary Cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz. Within each mode, a Design panel supports interactive layout construction, while an Error panel provides calibration analytics through four temporal viewing modes (Live, Snapshot, Intraday, and Multi-day range) together with threshold filtering and delta-mode comparison for drift identification. Each layout receives a Layout-Quality Score (LQS) that aggregates the readout and two-qubit gate errors of the layout into a single quality value. Starting from the automatic LUCJ circuit-generation provided by IBM Quantum, we extend it to a multi-programming setting in which multiple circuits are mapped onto a single quantum processing unit (QPU). I-QMapper further supports side-by-side visualization of two quantum backends and layout comparison, and session export for experimental reproducibility. By combining interactive exploration with calibration analytics, I-QMapper aims to support both rapid layout prototyping and informed noise-aware experimental design on NISQ devices.
tldr: I-QMapper is a Jupyter-based tool for noise-aware qubit layout selection and calibration analytics on NISQ hardware.
motivation: Achieving high-fidelity execution on NISQ hardware requires careful qubit layout selection, but existing tools lack integrated interactive visualization and calibration analytics.
method: The tool provides two modes (general-purpose and quantum-chemistry), interactive layout construction, calibration analytics with temporal viewing modes, and a Layout-Quality Score aggregating gate and readout errors.
result: I-QMapper enables rapid layout prototyping and informed noise-aware experimental design, supporting multi-programming and side-by-side backend comparison.
conclusion: The tool aims to improve qubit mapping and device diagnostics for NISQ hardware, but its contribution is primarily engineering and tool-building rather than advancing quantum information theory.

title: Bottleneck Effects And Harmonic-Type Velocity Bounds For Periodic Quantum Walks
authors: Houssam Abdul-Rahman, Thomas A. Jackson, Darren C. Ong
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove explicit upper bounds on the propagation velocity of one-dimensional quantum walks with periodic coins of arbitrary period. We treat two complementary settings. First, in a perturbative regime where one transmission parameter is small, we show that the corresponding almost reflecting coin acts as a bottleneck for transport: the velocity is bounded linearly in this parameter, with an explicit leading order estimate. Second, for arbitrary nonzero transmission parameters, we prove a general a priori bound in terms of their harmonic mean, together with a refined version that detects the spatial variation of neighboring coins. Moreover, we prove a general lower bound on the velocity. These bounds apply directly to the corresponding CMV setting.
tldr: This paper proves velocity bounds for periodic quantum walks, focusing on bottleneck effects and harmonic-type bounds.
motivation: Understanding propagation speed in quantum walks is important for quantum simulation and transport, but the paper's focus on specific periodic coin structures is narrow.
method: The authors use analytical techniques to derive upper and lower bounds on the group velocity for one-dimensional quantum walks with periodic coins, considering perturbative and general regimes.
result: They show that a small transmission parameter linearly bounds the velocity, and for arbitrary parameters, the velocity is bounded by the harmonic mean of transmission coefficients.
conclusion: The results provide explicit velocity bounds but are limited to periodic quantum walks, which are not a core topic in the user's research interests.

title: Quantum Typicality Survives non-Abelian Gauge Constraints: Exact Analytical Prediction Confirmed In $su(2)$ Lattice Gauge Theory
authors: Samuel L. Braunstein Zhi-Wei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Arguments for emergent spacetime require that quantum typicality, the generic absence of inter-subsystem correlations, persists on the physical Hilbert space of a gauge theory, where non-Abelian constraints could in principle inject geometry-supporting entanglement. Using [MATH] lattice gauge theory on two-dimensional tori ([MATH] up to [MATH]), we show that it does: the typical mutual information between strictly disjoint links matches an exact parameter-free analytical prediction combining a microcanonical baseline with Haar-random fluctuations. The Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian generates correlations from states of definite geometry (such as the electric vacuum), while generic states show only regression to the mean, establishing that the arrow of correlation growth requires a non-generic initial condition.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum typicality, i.e., the absence of correlations, persists in non-Abelian lattice gauge theory, with analytical predictions matching numerical simulations.
motivation: Understanding whether gauge constraints in non-Abelian theories can generate entanglement that supports emergent spacetime, and whether typicality holds in such constrained Hilbert spaces.
method: Analytical calculation of mutual information between disjoint links in SU(2) lattice gauge theory on a torus, using a microcanonical baseline and Haar-random fluctuations, compared with numerical simulations.
result: The typical mutual information matches the analytical prediction, showing that generic states have only regression to the mean, while the Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian generates correlations only from non-generic initial states.
conclusion: Quantum typicality survives non-Abelian gauge constraints, implying that the arrow of correlation growth requires a non-generic initial condition.

title: Fault Tolerant Computation Of The Static Structure Factor And Finite Size Effects
authors: Rishabh Bhardwaj, Alexander Reed Mu\~noz, Travis E. Jones, John Golden
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum algorithms offer a promising pathway for estimating the ground-state energies of periodic materials that are beyond the practical reach of classical electronic-structure methods. A remaining challenge is finite-size mitigation: quantum algorithms evaluate a finite supercell or finite Brillouin-zone mesh, while materials properties are defined in the thermodynamic limit. In this work we develop a quantum post-processing strategy for the leading two-body finite-size correction. After one-body shell effects are reduced by twist averaging, the dominant residual error is controlled by long-wavelength density fluctuations, which are encoded in the small-momentum static structure factor [MATH]. We formulate the corresponding operator in a Bloch-orbital basis, construct its block encoding through the density operator, and estimate its ground-state expectation value using an amplified Hadamard test. We also introduce adaptive global and local binary search procedures for identifying the infrared fitting window used to reconstruct the two-body finite size error correction. The resulting cost remains subleading relative to the main ground-state energy estimation routine: the structure-factor correction has leading [MATH] dependence on the Bloch-orbital basis size, avoids the large plane-wave prefactor of full Hamiltonian simulation, and requires only [MATH] logical qubits. This provides a fault-tolerant alternative to down-sampling, replacing repeated energy calculations on larger cells with targeted measurements of the infrared density correlations that control the finite-size effects.
tldr: This paper develops a fault-tolerant quantum algorithm to compute the static structure factor for finite-size corrections in periodic materials, using block encoding and amplified Hadamard test.
motivation: Quantum algorithms for ground-state energies of periodic materials suffer from finite-size errors; the dominant residual error after twist averaging is controlled by long-wavelength density fluctuations encoded in the static structure factor.
method: The authors formulate the structure factor operator in a Bloch-orbital basis, construct its block encoding via the density operator, and estimate its expectation value using an amplified Hadamard test. They also introduce adaptive binary search procedures for fitting the infrared window.
result: The correction cost scales as O(N^2) with Bloch-orbital basis size, avoids large plane-wave prefactors, and requires O(log N) logical qubits, remaining subleading relative to the main ground-state energy estimation.
conclusion: This provides a fault-tolerant alternative to down-sampling for finite-size mitigation, replacing repeated energy calculations on larger cells with targeted measurements of infrared density correlations.

title: Detector-Conditioned Source-Space Nulls And Null-Mask Loss In A Programmable Two-Slit Interferometer
authors: Jianming Wen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Afshar's double-slit experiment probes wave--particle complementarity by placing a wire grid at the dark fringes of a downstream interference pattern while retaining an imaging basis that appears to preserve which-path information. Here we propose and analyze a time-reversed Young--Afshar configuration in which the corresponding null test is transferred from the downstream field plane to the source-label plane of a time-reversed Young interferometer. In this reciprocal geometry, a point-addressable source illuminates a double slit, while the detector remains fixed. The observed fringe is therefore not a single-shot spatial intensity pattern, but a detector-conditioned response reconstructed by scanning the source coordinate. Consequently, a null in this pattern is not a node of a freely propagating field; it is a source label for which the coherent two-slit transfer amplitude to the selected detector vanishes. A mask placed at such source-plane labels is invisible to that detector when both slits are open, yet becomes visible when either slit is opened alone. We develop the scalar Fresnel model, derive the source-space null condition, introduce a detector-conditioned null-mask loss, and examine how this loss evolves under a tunable which-path marker. The source-space visibility and path distinguishability satisfy the standard duality relation, so no violation of complementarity is implied. The essential new feature is instead a reciprocal, detector-conditioned form of complementarity: Afshar's field-space transparency is replaced by response-function transparency in a reconstructed source basis.
tldr: This paper proposes a time-reversed Young-Afar configuration that transfers null tests to the source plane, exploring a reciprocal form of complementarity without violating standard duality relations.
motivation: To investigate wave-particle complementarity in a novel interferometric setup that challenges interpretations of Afshar's experiment.
method: The authors develop a scalar Fresnel model, derive source-space null conditions, and introduce a detector-conditioned null-mask loss, analyzing its evolution under a tunable which-path marker.
result: The source-space visibility and path distinguishability satisfy the standard duality relation, confirming no violation of complementarity; the new feature is a reciprocal, detector-conditioned form of complementarity.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical analysis of a reciprocal interferometer, but does not advance core quantum information topics such as entanglement, nonlocality, or quantum cryptography.

title: Quantum LiDAR With Non-local Modulation
authors: Xiao-Dong Fan, Zhong-Hua Ou, Yun-Ru Fan, Kai Guo, Zong-Liang Xie, Qiang Qi, Li-Xun Zhang, Si Shen, Hai-Zhi Song, Yan-Yu Wei, Hao Li, Li-Xing You, Qi Zhang, Yong Liu, Guang-Can Guo, Qiang Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum light detection and ranging (LiDAR) utilizes quantum entanglement and correlation to improve precision, noise resilience and covertness of target detection. Despite recent advances, the development of a quantum LiDAR system that simultaneously achieves high precision and a large measurement range remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a quantum amplitude-modulated continuous wave LiDAR with micrometer precision achievable via increased acquisition time and meter-scale measurement range. In our demonstration, the signal photons directly illuminate the target, while the idler photons are non-locally modulated with a high-frequency cosine wave and never interact with the target. By leveraging the non-local modulation and the quantum correlation, the target detection is achieved with a precision of 0.64 [MATH] 0.06 mm within one second over a measurement range of 2-8 m. As the acquisition time is up to 500 s, the system achieves a precision of 29 [MATH]. Furthermore, our system realizes a 50 times precision improvement over the classical single-photon scheme in a background noise 37 dB stronger than the returned probe photons. With these advantages, our method will open venues for the development of high-precision, long-range, and noise-resilient target detection.
tldr: Demonstrates a quantum LiDAR system using non-local modulation of idler photons to achieve high precision and noise resilience.
motivation: Existing quantum LiDAR systems struggle to simultaneously achieve high precision and large measurement range; the authors aim to overcome this trade-off.
method: Signal photons illuminate the target while idler photons are non-locally modulated with a high-frequency cosine wave; quantum correlation between them enables target detection.
result: Achieves 0.64 mm precision within 1 second over 2-8 m range, and 29 μm precision with 500 s acquisition; 50× precision improvement over classical scheme under strong noise.
conclusion: The non-local modulation approach enables high-precision, long-range, noise-resilient quantum LiDAR, opening new avenues for target detection.

title: Compression-Driven Anomaly Detection In Brain Mri Using An Interpretable Quantum Autoencoder
authors: Santanu Ganguly, Xing Liang, Dimitrios Makris
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a quantum autoencoder (QAE) for compression-driven anomaly detection in brain MRI data. The approach leverages angle encoding to map image patches into quantum states, followed by a variational encoder-decoder architecture trained to discard information via auxiliary trash qubits. Anomaly scores reflect the degree to which inputs resist compression relative to normal data, with higher scores corresponding to deviations from the learned normal manifold. Evaluated on publicly available brain MRI DICOM datasets, the method achieves a slice-level ROC-AUC of approximately 0.95 and a patch-level ROC-AUC of approximately 0.813, outperforming classical autoencoder and PCA baselines. Analysis of the learned parameters reveals a pronounced encoder-decoder asymmetry, where effective anomaly detection arises from structured information compression within the encoder rather than increased parameter magnitude or decoder expressivity. This results in a controlled compression-reconstruction trade-off with a clear operating regime that supports principled threshold selection. Qualitative evaluation further shows that the QAE produces spatially localized anomaly heatmaps aligned with tumorous regions. The results, supported by promising baseline performances, demonstrate that quantum autoencoders provide an interpretable and controllable mechanism for anomaly detection based on incompressibility with respect to a learned latent representation. This work highlights the potential of quantum autoencoders as a principled tool for studying compression dynamics in quantum machine learning, with promising implications for decision support in medical imaging workflows.
tldr: A quantum autoencoder is used for anomaly detection in brain MRI, achieving high ROC-AUC scores.
motivation: To leverage quantum machine learning for interpretable and controllable anomaly detection in medical imaging.
method: Angle encoding maps image patches to quantum states; a variational encoder-decoder with trash qubits learns to compress normal data; anomaly scores measure compression resistance.
result: Slice-level ROC-AUC ~0.95, patch-level ~0.813, outperforming classical baselines; encoder-decoder asymmetry observed.
conclusion: Quantum autoencoders offer a principled, interpretable mechanism for anomaly detection based on incompressibility, with potential for medical decision support.

title: Multi-parameter Two-photon Polarimetry At The Quantum Limit
authors: Joseph Niblo, Luca Maggio, Russell M. J. Brooks, Joseph Ho, Vincenzo Tamma, Alessandro Fedrizzi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic quantum metrology has demonstrated advantages in precision and resource efficiency for a wide range of applications, with several schemes approaching the fundamental quantum Cram\'er-Rao precision bound (QCRB). However, the intrinsic incompatibility of quantum measurements represents a hurdle in extending these advantages to the simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters. In this paper, we present an experimental protocol approaching the QCRB simultaneously in two polarisation parameters, across a wide range of the parameter space, with as few as [MATH] photon pairs, offering advantages for polarimetric sensing for dim sources such as in X-ray astronomy or photosensitive samples.
tldr: This paper presents an experimental protocol for multi-parameter two-photon polarimetry approaching the quantum Cramér-Rao bound.
motivation: Simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters in quantum metrology is hindered by measurement incompatibility; the authors aim to overcome this for polarimetric sensing.
method: They use two-photon polarization states and a measurement scheme designed to approach the quantum Cramér-Rao bound for two polarization parameters simultaneously.
result: The protocol achieves near-optimal precision across a wide parameter range with few photon pairs.
conclusion: This offers advantages for polarimetric sensing of dim sources, such as in X-ray astronomy or photosensitive samples.

title: Universal Framework For The Design Of Near-zero Refractive Index Photonic Crystals
authors: Micha\"el Lobet Adrien Debacq
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Near-zero-index (NZI) media are of great interest for controlling light-matter interactions, but homogeneous NZI materials in the telecom band remain limited and often suffer from significant losses. Photonic crystals provide an attractive alternative due to their tunability and use of low-loss constituent materials. This work presents a predictive framework for designing epsilon-near-zero (ENZ), mu-near-zero (MNZ), and epsilon-and-mu-near-zero (EMNZ) photonic crystals. We demonstrate an equivalence between Dirac cones and EMNZ behavior, showing that a Dirac cone at the Gamma point is both necessary and sufficient to obtain an effective EMNZ response under normal incidence. This result implies that the presence of a Dirac cone fully determines the NZI response of a photonic crystal, independent of the material composition. The prediction is based on mode symmetry universality and effective medium theory. The approach enables switching between ENZ-MNZ and EMNZ regimes through geometric tuning of the unit cell. It is validated on triangular and rectangular lattices. Overall, this work provides a predictive design strategy for NZI photonic crystals, replacing trial-and-error optimization. It may also impact metamaterials in the telecom regime and applications in quantum communication.
tldr: This paper presents a predictive framework for designing near-zero-index photonic crystals using Dirac cones and effective medium theory.
motivation: Homogeneous near-zero-index materials suffer from losses and limited availability; photonic crystals offer a tunable alternative but require systematic design rules.
method: The authors establish an equivalence between Dirac cones at the Gamma point and epsilon-and-mu-near-zero (EMNZ) behavior under normal incidence, using mode symmetry universality and effective medium theory.
result: They show that a Dirac cone is necessary and sufficient for EMNZ response, enabling switching between ENZ, MNZ, and EMNZ regimes via geometric tuning.
conclusion: This work provides a predictive design strategy for NZI photonic crystals, potentially impacting metamaterials and quantum communication applications.

title: Su(1,1) Symmetry And Exact Solutions Of The Dunkl-Klein-Gordon Equation In Higher Dimensions
authors: M. Salazar-Ram\'irez, B. C. L\"utf\"uo\u{g}lu, Jes\'us Alfredo Mart\'inez-Nu\~no
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the [MATH]-dimensional Dunkl--Klein--Gordon equation for a scalar particle within an algebraic framework. By employing Schr\"odinger factorization, we construct the generators of the [MATH] algebra and establish the associated symmetry of the radial sector. The energy spectrum is derived using irreducible unitary representations, and the corresponding Sturmian radial basis is obtained analytically. We analyze the [MATH]-dimensional Dunkl--Klein--Gordon oscillator and the bound-state sector of the [MATH]-dimensional Dunkl--Klein--Gordon equation with a Dunkl--Coulomb-like potential. Furthermore, [MATH] coherent states are constructed and their time evolution is analyzed, revealing a characteristic radial oscillation behavior. The results show that the Dunkl deformation introduces parity-dependent modifications in the spatial structure of the system while preserving its underlying algebraic dynamics.
tldr: This paper studies the Dunkl-Klein-Gordon equation in higher dimensions, deriving exact solutions and algebraic symmetries.
motivation: To understand the effects of Dunkl deformation on relativistic quantum systems and to find exact solutions for the Dunkl-Klein-Gordon equation.
method: Uses Schrödinger factorization to construct SU(1,1) algebra generators, derives energy spectrum via irreducible unitary representations, and obtains Sturmian radial basis analytically.
result: Obtains exact solutions for the Dunkl-Klein-Gordon oscillator and bound states with a Dunkl-Coulomb-like potential; constructs coherent states showing radial oscillations.
conclusion: The Dunkl deformation introduces parity-dependent modifications while preserving algebraic dynamics, but the work is not directly relevant to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Enhancing Co-packaging Optics Enabled Silicon Photonics Security Assurance Hardware Fingerprinting
authors: Liton Kumar Biswas, M Shafkat M Khan, Himanandhan Reddy Kottur, Hao Wang, Hamed Dalir, Navid Asadizanjani
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Silicon photonics enables integration of optical components using standard semiconductor processes, greatly improving data communication bandwidth and energy efficiency. However, photonics integrated circuits (PICs) face unique security challenges, such as counterfeit or tampering threats, that conventional electronic security methods do not address. We propose a novel hardware fingerprinting technique that embeds two dimensional photonic crystal patterns into the density control filler regions of a PIC. Each PhC pattern is designed to resonate a specific visible to near infrared wavelengths, producing a distinctive optical signature (based on wavelength, polarization, and incident angle) for each device. Finite difference time domain (FDTD) simulation using ANSYS Lumerical is employed to optimize nanostructure dimensions and spacing so that each device's reflection/absorption spectrum contains unique narrowband peaks. No extra fabrication steps or materials are required beyond standard lithography, keeping costs low. The embedded nanostructures have sub-50nm precision, making forgery extremely difficult. Our method yields a high resolution, scalable fingerprint for silicon photonic chips, enabling cost-effective device authentication and improved supply chain security.
tldr: This paper proposes a hardware fingerprinting technique for silicon photonic chips using embedded photonic crystal patterns.
motivation: Silicon photonics integrated circuits face unique security challenges like counterfeiting and tampering that conventional electronic methods do not address.
method: Two-dimensional photonic crystal patterns are embedded into density control filler regions of a PIC, designed to resonate at specific wavelengths, and simulated using FDTD to optimize dimensions.
result: The method yields unique narrowband reflection/absorption peaks for each device, enabling high-resolution, scalable fingerprinting without extra fabrication steps.
conclusion: This cost-effective authentication technique improves supply chain security for silicon photonic chips.

title: Quantum Dynamic Time Warping For Multivariate Time Series Classification
authors: Diego Alvarez-Estevez, Alejandro Mayorga-Redondo, Eduardo Mosqueira-Rey
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is a cornerstone for time series classification, but its reliance on Euclidean distances fails to capture latent cross-channel correlations in complex multivariate data. We propose a hybrid Quantum Dynamic Time Warping (qDTW) architecture, replacing the classical distance metric with the parameterized geometry of a quantum Hilbert space. Through structural ablation on benchmarks up to [MATH] spatial dimensions, we establish fundamental topological rules for quantum sequence alignment. We introduce a Unified Pre-Embedding Adjoint Ansatz that decouples trainable entanglement from classical data, eliminating the severe phase-scrambling and information bottlenecks inherent to traditional measurements. We demonstrate this decoupled architecture allows untrained quantum kernels to act as highly expressive baselines, while parameterized training effectively untangles deeply overlapping hyper-dimensional data. Furthermore, we identify a strict spatial-temporal expressivity tradeoff: temporal depth (data re-uploading) is necessary for dimensionally restricted univariate circuits, but applying it to wide multi-qubit registers triggers chaotic frequency-spectrum explosions and representation collapse. By navigating these topological hazards, our multivariate quantum architecture outperforms classical baselines, setting a new standard for integrating parameterized quantum circuits with dynamic programming.
tldr: Proposes a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for multivariate time series classification using quantum dynamic time warping.
motivation: Classical DTW fails to capture cross-channel correlations in multivariate time series; quantum Hilbert space geometry may provide a more expressive distance metric.
method: Replaces Euclidean distance in DTW with a parameterized quantum circuit distance, introduces a Unified Pre-Embedding Adjoint Ansatz to decouple entanglement from classical data, and analyzes spatial-temporal expressivity tradeoffs.
result: The quantum architecture outperforms classical baselines on benchmarks up to 8 spatial dimensions, with identified topological rules for quantum sequence alignment.
conclusion: Quantum DTW with proper architectural choices can surpass classical methods for multivariate time series classification, but careful design is needed to avoid representation collapse.

title: Parameter-Efficient Quantum-Inspired Fast Weight Programmers For Traffic-Matrix Forecasting
authors: Kuo-Chung Peng, Jiun-Cheng Jiang, Chun-Hua Lin, Tai-Yue Li, Nan-Yow Chen, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27821v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traffic matrices (TMs) capture network-wide origin-destination demand and are central to traffic engineering, yet accurate whole-matrix forecasting remains challenging when prediction must be performed under the memory, update, and training-budget constraints of online network control. This paper investigates whether compact quantum-inspired recurrent models can provide effective TM forecasts without relying on dedicated graph, transformer, or diffusion modules. We adapt gated quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold network fast-weight programmers (QKAN-FWPs) to direct multi-step Abilene TM forecasting, where each model predicts the next 20 five-minute frames of a 144-channel origin-destination (OD) matrix from a two-hour history. We benchmark three QKAN placement variants against a matched-size long short-term memory (LSTM) network, a larger LSTM, and a classical gated fast-weight programmer under a shared fixed-budget training protocol. Among the evaluated recurrent models, G-QKANFWP achieves the best pooled root-mean-square error (RMSE), while using only 22.4% of the larger LSTM. It also outperforms both the matched-size LSTM and the classical G-FWP baseline, indicating that the gain is not due to gated fast-weight framework alone. Convergence and channel-wise analyses further show that the quantum-inspired variants obtain lower validation-loss area under the learning curve (AULC) than matched-size recurrent baselines, while G-QKANFWP and GQKAN-FWP achieve substantially more OD-channel wins. These results identify a classical slow programmer with a quantum-inspired fast programmer as a promising accuracy-efficiency design for resource-conscious network traffic-matrix forecasting.
tldr: This paper applies quantum-inspired recurrent models to traffic-matrix forecasting, a classical networking task.
motivation: Accurate traffic-matrix forecasting under memory and update constraints is needed for online network control.
method: Gated quantum-inspired Kolmogorov-Arnold network fast-weight programmers (QKAN-FWPs) are adapted for multi-step forecasting of Abilene traffic matrices.
result: The best quantum-inspired variant (G-QKANFWP) achieves lower RMSE than larger LSTM baselines while using only 22.4% of the parameters.
conclusion: Quantum-inspired fast-weight programmers offer a promising accuracy-efficiency trade-off for resource-constrained traffic forecasting.

title: Survivor-conditioned Renewal Laws And Observable Bounds For Open Intermittent Maps
authors: Jason Duvall
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent numerical computations and stochastic modeling by Brevitt and Klages suggest that introducing a hole in a Pomeau--Manneville map can suppress survivor-conditioned Lyapunov stretching. We prove a deterministic renewal theorem which explains this phenomenon and its observable-level generalizations. For an open intermittent map induced on a base away from the neutral fixed point, we describe the asymptotic distribution of the number of completed survivor returns to the base, conditioned on survival up to time [MATH]. The limiting law is expressed in terms of the killed induced transfer operator; for the conditionally invariant density of the killed induced system it is geometric. We then prove two reward results for additive observables. A reward domination theorem gives bounded survivor-conditioned Birkhoff sums, while a stronger final-tail asymptotic gives convergence to a finite limit. For generalized Pomeau--Manneville maps, bounded observables satisfying [MATH] near the neutral fixed point and a mild variation condition satisfy the domination hypotheses. When the neutral branch and final tails satisfy the corresponding regularity assumptions, asymptotically regular observables satisfy the convergence hypotheses. In particular, [MATH] gives bounded survivor-conditioned Lyapunov stretching for the generalized class; under these additional regularity assumptions, it converges. Under an additional entropy-domination assumption, we also derive a zero entropy-rate consequence for survivor return-length names and record the complementary linear growth of stretching when the hole contains a neighborhood of the neutral fixed point.
tldr: This paper proves deterministic renewal theorems for open intermittent maps, focusing on survivor-conditioned Lyapunov stretching and observable bounds.
motivation: Recent numerical work suggested that introducing a hole in a Pomeau-Manneville map suppresses survivor-conditioned Lyapunov stretching; the authors aim to provide a rigorous explanation.
method: The authors use a killed induced transfer operator and prove renewal laws, reward domination, and final-tail asymptotic results for additive observables.
result: They show that survivor-conditioned Birkhoff sums are bounded and converge under certain regularity conditions, including bounded Lyapunov stretching for generalized Pomeau-Manneville maps.
conclusion: The work provides a deterministic foundation for observed stochastic behavior in open intermittent maps, with implications for understanding chaotic dynamics with holes.

title: Deriving Approximate Message Passing From The Convex Gaussian Min-Max Theorem
authors: Babak Hassibi Vikrant Malik
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Approximate message passing (AMP) provides fast iterative algorithms for high-dimensional signal recovery with Gaussian design matrices, while the Convex Gaussian Min-max Theorem (CGMT) gives a static optimization framework for obtaining sharp asymptotic characterizations of convex estimators. Although these two frameworks often lead to the same scalar state-evolution equations, their connection is usually indirect. In this paper, we establish a direct connection between the two for regularized linear regression in the proportional high-dimensional regime. When the CGMT Auxiliary Optimization (AO) and Primary Optimization (PO) give the same primal-dual solution, we show that the CGMT framework recovers the AMP fixed-point equations, including the Onsager correction. We further identify the AO Gaussian vectors with the Gaussian perturbations in the primal and residual AMP channels. For regularized M-estimation, the same viewpoint recovers the fixed point of scalar-variance max-sum Generalized AMP (GAMP). These results show that the AMP (and GAMP) iterations are suggested, and can be derived, from the CGMT framework, and may further suggest a way to derive AMP-like algorithms in settings where CGMT applies but standard AMP derivations are unavailable.
tldr: This paper establishes a direct connection between approximate message passing (AMP) and the convex Gaussian min-max theorem (CGMT) for regularized linear regression.
motivation: AMP and CGMT are two powerful frameworks for high-dimensional signal recovery, but their relationship was previously indirect. The authors aim to derive AMP iterations directly from CGMT.
method: The authors show that when the CGMT auxiliary and primary optimizations yield the same primal-dual solution, the CGMT framework recovers the AMP fixed-point equations including the Onsager correction. They also extend this to regularized M-estimation and generalized AMP.
result: The CGMT framework can be used to derive AMP and GAMP iterations, providing a unified perspective and potentially enabling new AMP-like algorithms in settings where CGMT applies.
conclusion: AMP algorithms can be derived from the CGMT framework, suggesting a systematic way to develop AMP-like methods for problems where standard AMP derivations are not available.

title: Constructions And Characterizations Of $s$-Plateaued Partitions
authors: Jiaxin Wang, Yadi Wei, Fang-Wei Fu, Jin Li, Fulin Li

title: Differential Privacy Over Hamming Codes
authors: Morteza Varasteh Borzoo Rassouli
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the transmission of the outputs of counting queries over a binary symmetric channel (BSC), where Hamming codes are employed as the channel encoder. Since the channel is inherently noisy, this transmission already provides a degree of privacy protection ``for free'', albeit at the cost of reduced utility in the form of decoding errors. A natural question is whether this privacy can be further improved (i) without any additional real-time obfuscation of the data, such as injecting artificial noise prior to transmission, and (ii) without increasing the end-to-end error probability. In this work, we answer this question in the affirmative by deriving an optimal codeword arrangement that strictly improves differential privacy guarantees while incurring no real-time computational overhead and no degradation in utility.
tldr: This paper studies differential privacy over Hamming codes for counting queries transmitted over a binary symmetric channel.
motivation: To improve differential privacy guarantees without additional obfuscation or increased error probability.
method: Derives an optimal codeword arrangement that leverages the inherent noise of the channel.
result: The optimal arrangement strictly improves differential privacy while maintaining utility.
conclusion: Privacy can be enhanced for free by careful codeword assignment in Hamming codes.

title: Prone: Petrov-Galerkin Operator Learning Unifies Dmd, SINDy & Koopmanism
authors: Matthew J. Colbrook, April Herwig, J. Nathan Kutz
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data-driven dynamics often asks how to linearize a nonlinear system. We ask instead: which observables should be advanced, and where should their futures live? This leads to Petrov Regression Of Nonlinear Evolution (PRONE), a Petrov--Galerkin regression framework based on [MATH] with distinct trial and test dictionaries. In this form, DMD, EDMD, SINDy, Koopman regression, sparse regression, and low-rank regression become variants of one construction: different dictionaries, weights, and constraints. We keep the linear algebra of Koopman learning, but drop the artificial requirement that a finite model map a dictionary into itself. With this asymmetry, eigenmodes are no longer the right objects. Instead, we use singular modes, which identify the observable combinations captured by the data, their projected futures, and the strength of the coupling between the two spaces. We identify the limiting projected operator and prove [MATH] convergence of the resulting nonlinear predictor. We give examples from chaotic maps, the double gyre, a pitching-airfoil wake, and Lorenz--63, where PRONE outperforms DeepONets, Fourier neural operators, and reservoir computers with considerably fewer parameters. These examples show the same message: lift once, regress once, and let the singular structure reveal statistics, transport, prediction, and dimension.
tldr: This paper introduces PRONE, a Petrov-Galerkin regression framework for data-driven dynamics that unifies DMD, SINDy, and Koopman methods.
motivation: The authors aim to linearize nonlinear systems by learning observables and their future evolution without requiring the finite model to map a dictionary into itself.
method: PRONE uses distinct trial and test dictionaries in a Petrov-Galerkin regression, dropping the self-mapping constraint of Koopman methods and employing singular modes instead of eigenmodes.
result: The method outperforms DeepONets, Fourier neural operators, and reservoir computers on chaotic maps, double gyre, pitching-airfoil wake, and Lorenz-63 with fewer parameters.
conclusion: The framework provides a unified perspective on several data-driven methods and demonstrates strong performance on nonlinear dynamics benchmarks.

title: The Multiply Iterated Law Of The Iterated Logarithm: Game-theoretic Foundations Of Sequential Detection Boundaries
authors: Akshay Balsubramani
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28324v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anytime-valid confidence sequences and e-processes are built almost universally from one recipe: average exponential test statistics over a prior on the tilting scale, then invoke Ville's inequality on the resulting nonnegative supermartingale. The mixing prior sets the width of the detection boundary and is usually chosen by hand. We recast the recipe as a two-player game with information as currency. A Learner commits to the prior; Nature adaptively produces a mean-zero score process whose difficulty is priced by a cumulant-generating-function charge. The Learner's mixture wealth obeys a single pathwise Gibbs-variational identity that holds along every realized path with no expectation operator; Ville's inequality, the equalizer condition, the GROW characterization, and the saddlepoint formula are all specializations of it. Three messages organize the rest. First, the law of the iterated logarithm (LIL) is the minimax boundary of this sequential-detection game, not arbitrary combinatorial slack. Second, the optimal prior is not a design choice but the forced equalizer strategy -- the unique law that makes every boundary-crossing time equally costly for Nature -- and it yields the sharp first iterated-log correction in closed form, with coefficient 3/2 = 1 + 1/2 (one for the Erds baseline, one half for the Laplace envelope around the saddle). Third, in the log-log scale chart the equalizer is exactly the Jeffreys prior on the scale-of-scales. The Erds-Kolmogorov integral test is the criterion that selects it. The two-stage finite-time LIL proof, the Howard-Ramdas mixture and stitching constructions, and betting confidence sequences all read as instances of this equalizer principle. A companion empirical evaluation confirms the central identities and locates the Erds threshold at the predicted value.
tldr: This paper develops game-theoretic foundations for sequential detection boundaries, deriving the law of the iterated logarithm as a minimax boundary and the optimal prior as an equalizer strategy.
motivation: Anytime-valid confidence sequences and e-processes rely on mixing priors chosen by hand; the paper seeks a principled, game-theoretic justification for the optimal prior and detection boundary.
method: The paper recasts the mixture recipe as a two-player game where a Learner commits to a prior and Nature produces a score process, using a pathwise Gibbs-variational identity to derive minimax boundaries.
result: The law of the iterated logarithm emerges as the minimax boundary, the optimal prior is the equalizer strategy with a sharp first iterated-log correction coefficient of 3/2, and the Jeffreys prior appears in log-log scale.
conclusion: The framework unifies existing constructions (Howard-Ramdas mixture, betting confidence sequences) under a single equalizer principle, providing a foundational perspective on sequential detection.

title: Operator Learning For Cubic Nonlinear Schr\"odinger Equation On Periodic Domains
authors: Emmanuel E. Oguadimma, Victory C. Obieke, Xueying Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27459v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider the cubic nonlinear Schr\"odinger (NLS) equation on two-dimensional flat tori with varying aspect ratios. In this formulation, the choice of aspect ratio governs the Fourier resonance structure, so rational and irrational geometries can exhibit different high-frequency cascade behaviors. We present a geometry-conditioned Fourier neural operator (FNO) for the cubic defocusing NLS equation, where the input consists of the real and imaginary parts of the solution together with the aspect-ratio parameter \(\omega^2\). The model is trained to approximate the one-step solution operator and is evaluated on unseen trajectories generated from random-phase initial data using Fourier pseudospectral method. Our numerical experiments show that the learned operator captures the main solution dynamics on both tori and reproduces the distinct Sobolev norm behavior of the two geometries, with stronger \(H^2\)-growth on the rational torus and more constrained behavior on the irrational torus, consistent with the findings of . We perform ablation studies to examine the roles of retained Fourier modes, activation functions, Fourier-layer depth, and explicit geometry conditioning. The results indicate that including [MATH] improves long-time predictive accuracy, especially for the rational geometry, and supports the use of geometry-aware neural operators for learning spectral-transfer phenomena in nonlinear dispersive partial differential equations.
tldr: This paper uses a Fourier neural operator to learn the solution operator of the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation on tori with varying aspect ratios.
motivation: To develop a geometry-conditioned neural operator that captures distinct high-frequency cascade behaviors on rational vs. irrational tori.
method: A Fourier neural operator is conditioned on the aspect ratio parameter and trained on pseudospectral simulation data to approximate the one-step time evolution.
result: The learned operator reproduces the different Sobolev norm growth behaviors on rational and irrational tori, with geometry conditioning improving long-time accuracy.
conclusion: Geometry-aware neural operators are effective for learning spectral-transfer phenomena in nonlinear dispersive PDEs.

title: When The Aggregator Cheats: Data-Free Backdoors In Federated LLM-based Qa Systems
authors: Chenqing Zhu, Yanbo Dai, Yulong Tian, Qingming Li, Songze Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based question-answering (QA) systems are increasingly deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare, mental health counseling, and legal consultation. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative training without sharing raw client data, for which locally trained models are aggregated at a central server (i.e., a cloud service provider) to obtain a global model. In this paper, we explore the potential vulnerability where a malicious aggregator, who may collude with a third-party vendor, stealthily implants advertisement-type backdoors into federated QA models, without ever accessing client data. The attacker's goals are twofold: (1) preserve clean QA fidelity (i.e., the poisoned model behaves like a clean model on non-triggered queries); and (2) generate highly natural, contextually relevant responses with target advertisements when a trigger appears. Achieving these two goals simultaneously is highly challenging, as naive backdoor injection without knowledge about private data may degrade model's clean performance or fail to inject the target. Motivated by this, we propose to leverage clients' uploaded gradients during training, and develop a two-stage framework for data-free and stealthy poisoning: (1) recover representative training samples from client gradients, and (2) construct poisoning datasets utilizing recovered samples and trigger phrases to inject backdoors into the global model. Experiments across representative QA datasets and LLM families under full fine-tuning and LoRA settings demonstrate that, our method achieves nearly 100% Attack Success Rate (ASR) while incurring negligible degradation on clean tasks. Crucially, reconstructing only 5-20% of gradients suffices to mount a reliable attack, exposing a practical blind spot in the pipeline of federated training of QA LLMs.
tldr: This paper proposes a data-free backdoor attack on federated LLM-based QA systems, where a malicious aggregator injects advertisement backdoors without accessing client data.
motivation: Federated LLM-based QA systems are vulnerable to backdoor attacks from a malicious aggregator who can collude with third parties to inject stealthy advertisement triggers.
method: The attacker recovers representative training samples from client gradients and constructs poisoning datasets using recovered samples and trigger phrases to inject backdoors into the global model.
result: The method achieves nearly 100% attack success rate with negligible degradation on clean tasks, requiring only 5-20% of gradients to mount a reliable attack.
conclusion: This exposes a practical blind spot in federated training of QA LLMs, highlighting the need for defenses against such data-free backdoor attacks.

title: Equivalence Of Continuous-Time Markov Chains And Linear Dynamical Systems
authors: Mihir Vahanwala
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The purpose of this short note is to record that an analogue of the following result, which is known for discrete-time linear dynamical systems, also holds in the continuous-time setting. The dynamics of a [MATH]-state Markov chain is governed by that of a linear dynamical system of dimension at most [MATH]; conversely, a linear dynamical system of dimension [MATH] can be "embedded" into a Markov chain with [MATH] states.
tldr: This note proves an equivalence between continuous-time Markov chains and linear dynamical systems, showing that the dynamics of an n-state Markov chain can be governed by a linear dynamical system of dimension at most n, and vice versa.
motivation: To extend a known discrete-time result to continuous-time, establishing a formal connection between two fundamental classes of dynamical systems.
method: The author constructs explicit mappings between the state space of a Markov chain and a linear dynamical system, using linear algebra and probability theory.
result: The equivalence holds in continuous-time: any n-state Markov chain corresponds to a linear dynamical system of dimension at most n, and any linear dynamical system of dimension n can be embedded into a Markov chain with n+1 states.
conclusion: The result bridges Markov chains and linear dynamical systems, potentially enabling cross-application of techniques between the two fields.

title: Reliable Homomorphic Matching For Fuzzy Labeled Psi At Scale
authors: Erkam Uzun
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27803v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fuzzy Labeled Private Set Intersection (FLPSI) lets a receiver learn the labels of enrolled records similar to its query, and nothing else. Constructions based on a set-threshold reduction reach practical performance: a query matches a record when the two agree on a threshold number of components, and the private matching is delegated to an inner set-threshold kernel. We study its homomorphic form, which combines leveled-BFV homomorphic encryption (HE), a garbled circuit, and secret sharing to decide the match under encryption and release the record's label. We identify a composition gap in this kernel: efficiency is bought with a per-trial false-accept probability, but one query runs a trial for every record, so the error compounds with the database size into the kernel's realization soundness error (RSE), the rate at which it accepts a query the plaintext matcher would reject. The RSE is a reliability property of the cryptographic matching layer, not the matcher's accuracy, and a sound kernel must contribute zero or negligible RSE of its own. We formalize this as a composable security property, give a closed-form bound on the receiver's advantage, and close the gap with CSTPSI, a kernel that runs independent token rounds and raises the per-trial bound to a matching power. We prove CSTPSI secure in the semi-honest model. The bound sets the round count: two token rounds suffice for million-scale databases and three for billion-scale at the [MATH] engineering threshold. Our evaluation confirms this: at a million records the baseline kernel's RSE reaches 100% while CSTPSI holds it at 0 in every measured configuration. For large labels at small to moderate scale CSTPSI is more than 20x faster than the baseline, with up to 93% less communication, converging to the baseline only at million-scale. Our implementation, with a one-command reproducibility harness, is publicly available.
tldr: This paper presents a homomorphic encryption-based protocol for fuzzy labeled private set intersection, focusing on cryptographic reliability and efficiency.
motivation: Existing fuzzy labeled private set intersection protocols suffer from a composition gap where per-trial false-accept probability compounds with database size, leading to unacceptable reliability errors.
method: The authors formalize the reliability soundness error (RSE) as a composable security property and propose CSTPSI, a kernel that runs independent token rounds to bound the error, using leveled-BFV homomorphic encryption, garbled circuits, and secret sharing.
result: CSTPSI achieves zero RSE in all measured configurations for million-scale databases, with up to 93% less communication and 20x faster performance for large labels at small to moderate scale.
conclusion: The proposed CSTPSI protocol closes the reliability gap in homomorphic matching for fuzzy labeled private set intersection, providing a sound and efficient solution for large-scale databases.

title: Self-Verifying Measurement Records: Hash-Linked Evidence Graphs For Hardware Benchmarking
authors: Baris Basaran Faruk Alpay
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Performance numbers reported for hardware are accepted on trust: the reader cannot recompute them, the apparatus is gone, and the silicon itself can be silently wrong, with fleet studies reporting on the order of one core in a thousand returning incorrect arithmetic with no error raised. We make a reported hardware measurement a tamper-evident, independently checkable record. Every quantity in the text, a table, or a figure is bound, by its content hash, to the observation and the verification behind it; the whole is a hash-linked, append-only structure (a transparency log for measurement) that a verifier audits offline without trusting its producer. Matrix products are verified by a probabilistic identity (Freivalds) at O(k n^2) cost under a tolerance we derive from floating-point error analysis and calibrate to the device's own measured residual floor, so a wrong product is rejected with probability 1 - 2^(-k); quantities with no such identity carry an algebraic checksum and a measured reproducibility class. We then treat the check itself as a security object: a probe seed committed for offline reproducibility is an attack surface, and a probe-aware adversary can hide a corruption in the probe's null space, fooling even a quorum of bit-identical witnesses, while a Fiat-Shamir challenge derived from the claimed output closes this. Driving the device from an unprivileged tenant's reach, with a di/dt power virus and a thermal soak, neither moves the calibrated tolerance nor produces a silent error, placing the physical-fault threat at the rare defective part or the privileged attacker and marking the boundary at which the record must compose with a hardware root of trust. We demonstrate the construction across Blackwell and Hopper GPUs and report a residual-floor and reproducibility map by precision, size, and device.
tldr: This paper proposes a tamper-evident, hash-linked evidence graph for verifying hardware measurement records, using probabilistic matrix product verification and Fiat-Shamir challenges.
motivation: Hardware performance numbers are often taken on trust, but silent errors in arithmetic are common; the paper aims to make measurements independently checkable and tamper-evident.
method: The authors bind each quantity in text, tables, or figures to its observation via content hashes in a hash-linked append-only structure. Matrix products are verified using Freivalds' algorithm with floating-point error tolerance, and other quantities carry algebraic checksums and reproducibility classes. A Fiat-Shamir challenge derived from the claimed output prevents probe-aware adversaries from hiding corruptions.
result: The construction is demonstrated on Blackwell and Hopper GPUs, showing that power viruses and thermal soaks do not produce silent errors, and a residual-floor and reproducibility map by precision, size, and device is reported.
conclusion: The method provides a practical way to create verifiable hardware measurement records, with the boundary for trust placed at rare defective parts or privileged attackers, requiring composition with a hardware root of trust.

title: Estimation--Prediction Tradeoff In Causal Probabilistic Temporal Graphs
authors: Aniq Ur Rahman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28225v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Temporal link prediction is usually evaluated by predictive performance on unseen edges, but in probabilistic temporal graphs this criterion can conflate model error with irreducible uncertainty. We study this issue by characterising an inherent estimation--prediction tradeoff in binary logistic models where regimes that maximise Fisher information and improve parameter recoverability are also those with the highest entropy, making individual predictions intrinsically harder even under perfect parameter recovery. We propose a probabilistic causal framework for generating temporal graphs with transient edges and known ground-truth causal structure, allowing temporal link prediction to be evaluated jointly with causal parameter recovery. For the proposed binary logistic parametrisation, we derive the Cram\'{e}r--Rao bound and validate the tradeoff between parameter estimation error and irreducible predictive loss. Our results show that predictive accuracy alone may not reflect whether a model has learned the underlying causal mechanism, motivating benchmarks that distinguish reducible model error from intrinsic process uncertainty.
tldr: This paper studies an estimation-prediction tradeoff in causal probabilistic temporal graphs, focusing on binary logistic models and temporal link prediction.
motivation: Temporal link prediction evaluation often conflates model error with irreducible uncertainty; the authors aim to separate these by characterizing a fundamental tradeoff between parameter estimation and prediction.
method: They propose a probabilistic causal framework for generating temporal graphs with known ground-truth causal structure, derive the Cramér-Rao bound for binary logistic parametrization, and validate the tradeoff between estimation error and predictive loss.
result: Regimes that maximize Fisher information and improve parameter recoverability also have highest entropy, making individual predictions harder even with perfect parameter recovery.
conclusion: Predictive accuracy alone may not reflect learning of the underlying causal mechanism; benchmarks should distinguish reducible model error from intrinsic process uncertainty.

title: Vector Representation Of Exact Soliton Dynamics In Multi-component Nonlinear Schr\"odinger Systems
authors: Maxime Foucher, Laurent Delisle, Amine Jaouadi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27569v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multicomponent nonlinear Schr\"odinger equations constitute fundamental models for coherent matter waves in multicomponent Bose--Einstein condensates, spinor quantum fluids, and vector nonlinear optical systems. We develop a vector formulation of the Hirota bilinear formalism for the completely integrable Manakov system that treats the coupled nonlinear Schr\"odinger equations directly at the vector level rather than through the conventional component-wise decomposition. This framework naturally retains the intrinsic multicomponent representation of the model while providing compact analytical expressions for exact vector soliton solutions. Within this approach, we systematically construct bright, dark, and mixed one-, two-, and three-soliton solutions and show how the underlying vector structure provides a unified description of their nonlinear interactions. In particular, the proposed formalism makes the coupling between the different components explicit while preserving the geometric organization of the vector system throughout the bilinearization procedure. Beyond its analytical simplicity, the framework offers a natural perspective for the study of coherent multicomponent nonlinear excitations and provides a foundation for extending vector Hirota methods to other classes of exact solutions, including rogue waves, periodic waves, and rational solutions.
tldr: This paper develops a vector formulation of the Hirota bilinear method for the Manakov system, providing exact soliton solutions for multicomponent nonlinear Schrödinger equations.
motivation: To treat coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equations directly at the vector level, preserving the multicomponent structure and simplifying the derivation of exact soliton solutions.
method: A vector generalization of the Hirota bilinear formalism is applied to the completely integrable Manakov system, constructing bright, dark, and mixed soliton solutions up to three solitons.
result: Compact analytical expressions for vector soliton solutions are obtained, with explicit coupling between components and a unified description of nonlinear interactions.
conclusion: The vector framework offers analytical simplicity and a foundation for extending Hirota methods to other exact solutions like rogue waves and periodic waves.

title: Vibrational High-harmonics And Period-doubling Bifurcation Probed By Time-resolved Electron Diffraction
authors: Alexander Schr\"oder, Kai Nettersheim, Ferdinand Evers, Sascha Sch\"afer
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nanoscale mechanical oscillators exhibit a plethora of nonlinear phenomena with promising applications for the sensing and clocking of processes down to atomic length scales. Oscillator dynamics are typically probed by electrical or optical means, providing only limited access to the spatial profile of the oscillator motion. Here, we introduce event-based convergent beam electron diffraction for the spatio-temporal mapping of nanoscale mechanical resonators in ultrafast transmission electron microscopy. Employing an optically driven silicon membrane resonator at various driving strengths, we gain access to nonlinear processes with increasing complexity, ranging from a simple Duffing behavior to nonlinear multimode coupling and period-doubling bifurcations. The time-resolved diffraction probing approach supports a spatial resolution down to a few nanometers and a temporal resolution of 5 ns and provides quantitative information on the local membrane bending. Because the diffraction signal responds to local displacement gradients, which become more pronounced as resonators shrink, this approach offers a route toward probing nonlinear nanomechanics at the atomic scale.
tldr: This paper uses time-resolved electron diffraction to study nonlinear dynamics in nanomechanical resonators.
motivation: Understanding nonlinear phenomena in nanoscale oscillators is important for sensing and clocking applications, but existing probing methods lack spatial resolution.
method: The authors introduce event-based convergent beam electron diffraction in ultrafast transmission electron microscopy to map the spatio-temporal motion of an optically driven silicon membrane resonator.
result: They observe nonlinear processes including Duffing behavior, multimode coupling, and period-doubling bifurcations, achieving nanometer spatial and 5 ns temporal resolution.
conclusion: This diffraction-based approach provides quantitative local bending information and could enable probing nonlinear nanomechanics at atomic scales.

title: Nonextensive Statistical Signatures Of The Bilaterian Transition In Proteome Length Distributions
authors: Sertac Eroglu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein length distributions across the tree of life carry a quantitative signature of organismal complexity. Nonextensive statistical mechanics, through the Tsallis generalized entropy formalism, provides a natural framework for describing complex systems characterized by long-range correlations, scale invariance, and hierarchical organization -- features that classical Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics cannot accommodate. In this work, the complementary cumulative distribution function (CCDF) of protein lengths is analyzed within this framework for the reference proteomes of 22 fully sequenced organisms spanning the domains Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya, with deliberate sampling across the animal transition zone from sponges and cnidarians to higher bilaterians. Maximum likelihood (MLE) fitting of truncated discrete q-exponential distributions, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs) reveals that the entropic index q resolves into three statistically distinct regimes: superextensive (q < 1) for prokaryotes, unicellular and non-animal multicellular eukaryotes, and basal animals; a boundary regime (CI on spanning unity) for the two cnidarians studied and the basal bilaterian C. teleta; and subextensive (q > 1) for all higher bilaterians, with q increasing monotonically across the four deuterostomes sampled from S. purpuratus (1.033) to H. sapiens (1.147). The q-exponential outperforms the ordinary exponential distribution across all 22 proteomes and becomes progressively more competitive against alternative two-parameter distributions as proteome complexity increases. These results identify the Tsallis entropic index as a continuous, physically interpretable indicator of proteome organizational complexity and extend the applicability of nonextensive statistical mechanics to proteomic systems.
tldr: This paper applies nonextensive statistical mechanics to analyze protein length distributions across species, identifying the Tsallis entropic index as a marker of organismal complexity.
motivation: To find a quantitative signature of organismal complexity in proteome length distributions that classical Boltzmann-Gibbs statistics cannot capture.
method: Fits truncated discrete q-exponential distributions to complementary cumulative distribution functions of protein lengths for 22 organisms using maximum likelihood estimation with bootstrap confidence intervals.
result: The entropic index q resolves into three regimes: superextensive (q<1) for prokaryotes and basal animals, boundary (q≈1) for cnidarians and a basal bilaterian, and subextensive (q>1) for higher bilaterians, increasing monotonically with complexity.
conclusion: The Tsallis entropic index serves as a continuous, physically interpretable indicator of proteome organizational complexity, extending nonextensive statistical mechanics to proteomic systems.

title: Fast-Mixing Markov Chains Without Gradients
authors: Robert Scheichl Robert Kutri
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most approaches for accelerating Markov chain mixing either rely on incorporating expensive geometric information in the proposals, or reduce the per-step cost of sampling via surrogate densities. We propose a localisation principle that allows a surrogate-based Metropolis-Hastings proposal to exploit gradient-level geometric information of the target density, without evaluating either the target gradient or the surrogate gradient. The construction relies on regularisation and tempering of the proposal measure. We show that the expected proposal displacement coincides with the Langevin drift up to controlled error. The resulting framework, Delayed Acceptance with Regularisation and Tempering (DART), achieves an [MATH] mixing time from warm start for strongly log-concave targets with condition number [MATH] in [MATH] dimensions. This matches the known [MATH] rate for MALA when [MATH], and scales as [MATH], independent of dimension, otherwise. This is, to our knowledge, the first mixing time guarantee for a surrogate-transition-based MCMC method. We demonstrate DART on a hierarchical spatial generalised linear mixed model. In this setting, the Dirichlet-Neumann averaging parametrisation, originally introduced for the efficient simulation of Gaussian processes, is repurposed to supply the surrogate, and its linear memory and log-linear arithmetic scaling in the number of observation sites carry over to inference.
tldr: This paper proposes a gradient-free MCMC method using surrogate densities and regularization to achieve fast mixing for strongly log-concave targets.
motivation: Accelerating Markov chain mixing typically requires expensive gradient information or surrogate densities; the authors aim to achieve fast mixing without evaluating gradients of the target or surrogate.
method: They introduce a localisation principle that allows a surrogate-based Metropolis-Hastings proposal to exploit gradient-level geometric information via regularization and tempering, without explicit gradient computation.
result: The method achieves O(κ^2 d log(κ)) mixing time from warm start for strongly log-concave targets, matching MALA when κ=O(1) and scaling as O(d log d) otherwise.
conclusion: DART provides the first mixing time guarantee for surrogate-transition-based MCMC and demonstrates practical efficiency on a hierarchical spatial GLMM.

title: Policy Gradient Learning For Distributionally Robust Markov Decision Processes Under Wasserstein Ambiguity
authors: Yadh Hafsi, Samy Mekkaoui, Huy\^en Pham, Kaixin Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) under distributional uncertainty in the transition kernels and develop a policy-gradient framework for Wasserstein distributionally robust control. Ambiguity is modeled by state-action dependent Wasserstein balls around nominal transition kernels, leading to a max-min control problem over randomized policies and admissible transition laws. Since the worst-case transition law depends implicitly on the policy parameters, the usual policy-gradient argument does not apply. We address this difficulty by using a Wasserstein dual reformulation of the robust Bellman recursion and analyzing its directional differentiability. This yields an explicit recursive characterization of the robust policy gradient. Building on this characterization, we propose a robust actor-critic algorithm and illustrate its behavior on discrete and continuous benchmark examples.
tldr: This paper develops a policy-gradient framework for distributionally robust Markov decision processes under Wasserstein ambiguity, focusing on robust control in operations research.
motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of optimizing policies in MDPs when transition kernels are uncertain, modeled by Wasserstein balls, which is a problem in robust optimization and control theory.
method: The authors derive a robust policy gradient using a Wasserstein dual reformulation of the robust Bellman recursion and analyze its directional differentiability, then propose a robust actor-critic algorithm.
result: They provide an explicit recursive characterization of the robust policy gradient and demonstrate the algorithm on discrete and continuous benchmark examples.
conclusion: The work contributes to distributionally robust reinforcement learning but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Performance Analysis And Optimal Design Of ORB-Type Grand Algorithms
authors: Wenyi Zhang Li Wan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28030v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Guessing Random Additive Noise Decoding (GRAND) performs decoding by sequentially guessing channel error patterns (EPs). Ordered Reliability Bits GRAND (ORBGRAND) is a notable instance suitable for efficient implementation, as it schedules EPs solely according to the ranking of soft channel outputs. In this paper, we generalize this principle to a broader class of GRAND algorithms whose testing order depends only on reliability ranking, referred to as ORB-type GRAND. We develop a unified analytical framework based on a key quantity termed the average guessing posterior (AGP), which captures the effectiveness of each EP and reduces decoding into an ordering problem over the EP space. For random code ensembles, we derive exact expressions for the block error rate (BLER), stopping-time distribution, and average number of tests under a fixed test budget. The analysis separates target-miss and target-preemption errors and shows that ordering EPs by non-increasing AGP is optimal over the EP set under consideration.
